title: Supreme Court Allows Trump to End Protections for Haitian and Syrian Immigrants
summary:
On Thursday, the Supreme Court handed the Trump administration a major victory. By a 6-to-3 vote along ideological lines, the court ruled that President Trump has virtually unrestrained power to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) program for hundreds of thousands of immigrants. The decision applies specifically to people from Haiti (about 330,000) and Syria (about 3,800), but could set a precedent for other countries.

TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to allow migrants from countries affected by natural disasters or armed conflicts to live and work legally in the U.S. Until Trump, every president—Republican and Democrat—had embraced it. The Trump administration argued that the program was meant to be temporary and that the president has the authority to end it. Justice Samuel Alito, writing for the conservative majority, agreed, saying the law gives the president unreviewable authority.

Dissenting were the court's three liberal justices. Immigrant rights groups reacted with outrage. Todd Schulte of FWD.us called the decision "cruel" and "economic self-sabotage." According to his group, 200,000 Haitian TPS holders are in the U.S. workforce, including 15,000 agricultural workers, 13,000 nursing assistants, and 8,000 caregivers. They generate $5.9 billion for the economy and pay $1.5 billion in taxes annually.

The decision means that Haitians and Syrians will likely lose their legal status, jobs, and face deportation. Many will have to leave their American-born children behind. The administration had already stripped TPS from 13 of 17 countries. The remaining four—El Salvador, Lebanon, Sudan, and Ukraine—may lose their status when it comes up for renewal this fall.
why_it_matters: This ruling affects real people—classmates, neighbors, or workers—who may be forced to leave the only home they have known, reshaping communities and highlighting the tension between presidential power and human rights.

background_read: Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was established by Congress in 1990 as a humanitarian program for migrants who cannot safely return home due to natural disasters or armed conflicts. The Supreme Court of the United States—the nation's highest judicial body, currently with a 6-3 conservative majority—can strike down or uphold executive actions on immigration. President Donald Trump (who returned to the White House in January 2025) has pursued strict immigration limits throughout his second term. Haiti has suffered from a catastrophic 2010 earthquake and ongoing gang violence, while Syria has been torn by civil war since 2011, creating millions of refugees. The ruling declares that the president's power to end TPS is virtually unreviewable, meaning federal courts cannot second-guess the decision. Advocacy group FWD.us—founded by technology leaders to push for immigration reform—said the move would remove tens of thousands of workers from essential industries like farming and healthcare, costing the U.S. economy billions. The decision could also affect immigrants from El Salvador, Lebanon, Sudan, and Ukraine, whose TPS designations expire later this year.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — Supporters of strong executive power
perspectives.description: They argue the president needs broad authority to enforce immigration laws, and that TPS was always meant to be a short-term fix, not a permanent pathway to residency.
They say the decision is cruel, breaks up families, and removes essential workers from the labor force, harming the U.S. economy and abandoning people from countries still in crisis.

This ruling significantly expands presidential power over immigration, limiting the role of courts in reviewing such decisions—a shift that could affect future policies on refugees and asylum seekers.

If the administration ends TPS for the remaining four countries, hundreds of thousands more could lose legal status, and Congress may face pressure to craft a permanent solution for long-term TPS holders.
